source.title: The Benefits of Implicit Regularization from SGD in Least Squares Problems
source.authors: Difan Zou; Jingfeng Wu; V. Braverman; Quanquan Gu; Dean Phillips Foster; S. Kakade

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; no apparent truncation or garbling affecting the reported results.
record.tranche_reason: The paper analyzes implicit regularization in least squares and reports its own theory and experiments comparing SGD with explicit ridge regularization. Its results qualify claims about SGD's generalization advantage by showing this comparison depends on problem instances, sample sizes, and tuning; it does not test natural-label deep-network generalization or memorization of random labels.
record.gate_note: Theoretical comparisons and the six-instance Gaussian experiment bear on implicit versus explicit regularization. Cited results about deep networks and prior work are not this paper's own results. No measured natural-label test-error comparison for deep networks is reported.
record.test_reason: The study compares tuned, tail-averaged SGD with ridge regression on linear least-squares problems. None of V1–V8 concerns that comparison. In particular, ridge regression is not an adaptive optimizer, so these results do not test V4. References to deep-network generalization provide motivation rather than tests of the listed versions.
record.authors_conclusion: The record broadly captures the authors' conclusion. More precisely, they establish constant-factor risk competitiveness of tuned, single-pass, tail-averaged SGD against ridge, with logarithmic sample inflation for specified broad problem classes; the general Gaussian bound also depends on signal-to-noise ratio and covariance spectrum. Some constructed instances yield nearly quadratic sample advantages for SGD. These conclusions concern linear least squares, including underparameterized and overparameterized regimes.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies one-pass, constant-stepsize tail-averaged SGD versus explicitly regularized ridge regression on synthetic least-squares problems, rather than deep-network recipes or adaptive optimizers.
record.method_sensitivity: The comparison varies with data distribution (one-hot or Gaussian), covariance spectrum, signal-to-noise ratio, ground-truth parameter structure, and sample size; the SGD stepsize is tuned.

fits_no_version.finding: Tuned tail-averaged SGD is competitive with ridge on one-hot problems at the same sample size and on Gaussian problems under instance-dependent sample inflation; some structured Gaussian cases permit equal-sample competitiveness.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For specified linear least-squares problem classes, tuned SGD matches ridge's expected excess risk up to constant factors with a controlled increase in sample size.

fits_no_version.finding: Across six synthetic Gaussian instances, the authors report a nearly constant-factor sample disadvantage for SGD with uniform ground-truth coefficients and substantial advantages when the signal concentrates in leading eigendirections.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The relative sample efficiency of tuned SGD and ridge depends on covariance spectrum and signal alignment.

fits_no_version.finding: A constructed Gaussian instance gives a nearly quadratic sample-efficiency separation favoring SGD over optimally tuned ridge.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Some Gaussian least-squares instances require ridge to use nearly quadratically more samples than tuned SGD for comparable excess risk.

record.problems: The empirical section uses six synthetic Gaussian least-squares instances, dimension d = 200, and 20 independent runs; text gives qualitative curve descriptions without numeric plotted values or error bars. The central comparisons are theoretical bounds under stated assumptions, not deep-network experiments.
record.rows_left_out: No results omitted. Figure 1's six conditions are recorded separately; exact values are not stated in the text.

untested.parts: Coexistence of random-label fitting and natural-label held-out accuracy in the same neural architectures and training recipes.
Test error as neural-network width increases beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image-classification performance and the contribution of local connectivity.
All parts: adaptive optimizers versus SGD or momentum SGD, tuning budgets, benchmark performance, and recovery through weight decay or optimizer switching.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and changes to training duration or recipes.
Dropout effects on classifier test error, including training-set size, underfitting, augmentation, and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness ranking generalization gaps relative to norm- and margin-based measures.
Test-accuracy effects of removing highly memorized training examples compared with random removal.

record.verdict_notes: Remove both proposed V4 verdicts. Comparing SGD with ridge cannot support or limit a claim about adaptive optimizers versus SGD. All row states are cannot_determine relative to the listed versions because their measures do not address those versions.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label test accuracy in deep networks.
Widening one-hidden-layer ReLU networks past interpolation on MNIST or downsampled CIFAR-10.
Convolutional versus fully connected image-network generalization.
Adaptive optimizers, image and language benchmarks, and comparisons with SGD or momentum under limited or broader tuning; the paper compares SGD only with ridge regression in least squares.
Large-batch versus small-batch training and adaptation of epoch budgets or recipes.
Dropout, weight decay, and augmentation interventions in classifiers.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and other measures tracking train-test gaps.
Removing high-influence memorized examples and measuring test-accuracy changes.

rows.subject: SGD with tail-averaging
rows.operation_detail: Theoretical instance-wise comparison with ridge regression on one-hot least squares; tuned constant stepsize.
rows.measure: Expected excess risk relative to ridge regression
rows.baseline: ridge excess risk at Nridge and λ
rows.value: SGD excess risk . ridge excess risk < σ²
rows.note: Theoretical bound; the paper states that with the same or more samples SGD is competitive with ridge on every one-hot instance.
rows.check: SGD versus ridge does not measure V4. The theorem establishes competitiveness up to an absolute constant factor, not necessarily equal or smaller risk.

rows.subject: SGD with tail-averaging
rows.operation_detail: Theoretical instance-wise comparison with ridge regression on Gaussian least squares; tuned constant stepsize.
rows.measure: Expected excess risk relative to ridge regression
rows.baseline: ridge excess risk at Nridge and λ
rows.value: SGD excess risk . ridge excess risk
rows.note: A bound on required samples for tuned SGD to match ridge; the sample requirement depends on signal-to-noise and covariance-spectrum flatness.
rows.check: This sample-inflation guarantee compares SGD with ridge, not adaptive optimizers with SGD. Its additional sample requirement is not partial evidence for V4.

rows.subject: SGD with tail-averaging
rows.operation_detail: Theoretical comparison for Gaussian least squares with polynomially decaying spectrum and bounded signal-to-noise ratio.
rows.measure: Expected excess risk relative to any ridge solution in generalizable regime
rows.note: The paper's stated sufficient-condition result for this class of instances.
rows.check: The polynomial-spectrum least-squares guarantee measures none of the listed versions; risk competitiveness is up to constant factors.

rows.subject: SGD with tail-averaging
rows.operation_detail: Theoretical comparison for Gaussian least squares with random, rotation-invariant ground-truth parameter.
rows.measure: Expected excess risk relative to any ridge solution in generalizable regime
rows.note: Expected risk includes expectation over random data and random ground truth.
rows.check: No adaptive optimizer is tested. The conditions also omit those inherited from Corollary 5.1: bounded signal-to-noise ratio, d = O(Nridge), and the specified polynomial spectrum. Risk is averaged over both data and random ground truth.

rows.subject: SGD with tail-averaging
rows.operation_detail: Theoretical comparison for Gaussian least squares when the ground truth has limited tail-eigenspace mass.
rows.measure: Expected excess risk relative to generalizable ridge solutions
rows.value: SGD excess risk . ridge excess risk
rows.note: A sufficient condition for SGD to outperform or match ridge at the same sample size.
rows.check: This is an SGD–ridge comparison, unrelated to V4. The stated tail-mass condition sums from k* + 1 through Nridge, not through the entire remaining spectrum. The guarantee is up to constant factors.
